results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.key_finding: Empiric regimens for adults aged >50 years or with immunocompromised state must include ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours to cover Listeria monocytogenes, in addition to vancomycin plus ceftriaxone. Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins. Treatment duration for Listeria meningitis is 21 days of ampicillin (with or without gentamicin in the first week for synergy). Adjunctive dexamethasone has the strongest evidence in pneumococcal meningitis; its role in Listeria meningitis is less established but is used in practice.
results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis

results.authors: Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D.
results.key_finding: Listeria monocytogenes accounts for approximately 4% of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults but is a leading organism in adults over 60 years and in the immunocompromised. Dietary exposure to unpasteurised dairy products and deli meats is a recognised risk factor. Case fatality rate is approximately 20-30%. Listeria is uniformly resistant to cephalosporins; ampicillin (or penicillin G) is the drug of choice. Trim-sulfamethoxazole is used in penicillin-allergic patients.
results.title: Community-Acquired Bacterial Meningitis in Adults

results.authors: De Gans J, van de Beek D.
results.key_finding: Adjunctive dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days) significantly reduced unfavourable outcomes and mortality in adults with bacterial meningitis, with the greatest benefit in patients with pneumococcal meningitis. Benefit in Listeria meningitis was not independently powered. Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics.
results.title: Dexamethasone in Adults with Bacterial Meningitis

results.authors: van de Beek D et al.
results.key_finding: For empiric meningitis therapy in older adults and immunocompromised patients, ampicillin must be added to cover Listeria monocytogenes. Cephalosporins are not active against Listeria. TMP-SMX 5 mg/kg IV every 6 hours is recommended for penicillin-allergic patients. Treatment duration for confirmed Listeria meningitis is at least 21 days.
results.title: ESCMID Guideline for Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute Bacterial Meningitis

output.summary: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis predominantly affects older adults (>60 years) and immunocompromised patients, including those on corticosteroids. Dietary exposure to unpasteurised dairy is a documented risk factor. Listeria is uniformly cephalosporin-resistant; ampicillin (or penicillin G) is the cornerstone of definitive therapy, with TMP-SMX as an alternative in penicillin allergy. Empiric regimens in at-risk adults must therefore include ampicillin in addition to standard vancomycin plus ceftriaxone. Treatment duration is at least 21 days. The role of adjunctive dexamethasone in Listeria meningitis is less established than in pneumococcal disease.

alternatives: TMP-SMX 5 mg/kg IV every 6 hours can replace ampicillin if penicillin allergy is confirmed (not applicable here); meropenem 2 g IV every 8 hours is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

Vancomycin + CKD: In chronic kidney disease, vancomycin requires AUC-guided dosing and enhanced renal function monitoring; creatinine at baseline is mildly elevated.
Ampicillin: No significant interactions with current medications.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT rely on ceftriaxone alone to cover Listeria monocytogenes — Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins; ampicillin is mandatory.
Do NOT delay empiric ampicillin-inclusive antibiotic therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (age >60, altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, seizure) is present.

Do NOT attribute CSF pleocytosis exclusively to methotrexate-associated aseptic meningitis without culture and PCR confirmation — Gram-positive rods and positive culture exclude drug-induced aseptic meningitis.

required_recommendations: Administer empiric IV antibiotics (ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours + vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV + ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; ampicillin is MANDATORY for Listeria coverage in this immunocompromised patient over 60.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue every 6 hours for 4 days.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain non-contrast CT head before LP given age >60, altered mental status, and immunocompromised status.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose with paired serum glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, CSF lactate) at LP.
Hold methotrexate during the acute illness and dexamethasone course; monitor LFTs.

Place patient on droplet precautions until Listeria confirmed (not droplet-transmitted, but until meningococcal disease excluded).

differential.key_features: Would show lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis with normal or mildly elevated protein and normal glucose; procalcitonin and CRP would be much lower; Gram stain and culture negative
Subacute or chronic onset over weeks; lymphocytic CSF with very low glucose and high protein is similar, but AFB stain/culture and TB PCR would distinguish; onset here is acute (48h)
More indolent course; typically in severely immunocompromised (HIV, solid organ transplant); cryptococcal antigen/India ink would be diagnostic; this patient's immunosuppression is modest
Methotrexate-associated aseptic meningitis occurs but typically yields sterile lymphocytic CSF; culture-positive Gram-positive rods and markedly elevated procalcitonin exclude this

key_clinical_evidence: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis predominantly affects adults over 60 and immunocompromised patients, including those on corticosteroids or disease-modifying agents; this patient meets both criteria.

Dietary exposure to unpasteurised soft cheese is the classic risk factor for Listeria acquisition; the history of such exposure three weeks prior is temporally consistent with incubation and presentation.

Listeria is uniformly resistant to cephalosporins; failure to include ampicillin in the empiric regimen would leave the causative organism uncovered despite an otherwise appropriate vancomycin + ceftriaxone backbone.

The CSF pattern (neutrophilic pleocytosis, very low glucose ratio, markedly elevated protein, positive Gram stain for Gram-positive rods) is consistent with bacterial infection; multiplex PCR and culture confirming Listeria monocytogenes establishes the diagnosis.
CT head before LP is mandatory: this patient is aged >60, immunocompromised, and has altered mental status — three independent imaging-first criteria per IDSA 2004.
Drug-induced aseptic meningitis from methotrexate is a red herring: it produces a sterile lymphocytic CSF, whereas this CSF shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with a positive Gram stain and culture.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Drug-induced aseptic meningitis from methotrexate produces a sterile lymphocytic pleocytosis, not neutrophilic pleocytosis with Gram-positive rods on Gram stain and a positive culture; the CSF findings unambiguously favour bacterial infection over a drug-induced process.
red_herrings.data_point: Methotrexate in the medication list as a potential cause of drug-induced aseptic meningitis
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent anchored on the medication list might consider drug-induced aseptic meningitis from methotrexate and underweight the bacterial diagnosis, potentially delaying empiric antibiotics.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present. This patient meets multiple criteria: age >60, altered mental status, and immunocompromised state (prednisone + methotrexate). LP in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward: classic presentation with fever, headache, meningismus, altered mental status, positive Gram stain and culture. patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Carmela Esposito is a 78-year-old right-handed retired schoolteacher with rheumatoid arthritis on low-dose prednisone and methotrexate who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after 48 hours of worsening confusion, high fever, and neck stiffness. Her daughter reports that two days ago, Mrs. Esposito called complaining of a severe headache she described as 'the worst headache of her life' and generalised malaise. Her temperature at home was 38.4 degrees Celsius. The daughter gave her acetaminophen 1000 mg and attributed the symptoms to a possible viral illness given mild nasal congestion the patient had noted over the preceding week. Overnight, the patient's confusion worsened markedly. This morning, her daughter found her lying in bed, unable to recognise her, not knowing what year it was, and complaining bitterly of photophobia and neck pain. She was unable to stand without assistance. The daughter also reports that Mrs. Esposito has a history of consuming unpasteurised soft cheeses, and approximately three weeks prior to this presentation she had eaten a locally sourced soft cheese at a family gathering. There was no witnessed seizure activity, no rash, and no recent sick contacts with meningitis. The patient has been on prednisone 7.5 mg daily and methotrexate 15 mg weekly for rheumatoid arthritis for approximately four years. Her last rheumatology visit one month ago documented well-controlled disease. She has no history of prior CNS infection, neurosurgical procedures, or cerebrospinal fluid leak. On arrival to the ED she was febrile at 39.1 degrees Celsius, tachycardic, lethargic, and in moderate distress from photophobia and neck pain.

Kernig sign positive bilaterally with resistance and pain on knee extension from 90 degrees hip flexion. Brudzinski sign positive with involuntary lower-extremity flexion on passive neck flexion. No petechial or purpuric rash on skin examination. No focal dermatological source of infection. Left knee prosthesis site without erythema, swelling, or warmth.

Hearing grossly reduced bilaterally, attributed to baseline age-related presbycusis. Gag reflex intact. Tongue midline.
